options: Stack: last in, FIRST out. Queue: first in, first out
explanation: Plates vs checkout line. The restriction IS the feature - with one reachable item, whole bug categories vanish.
Push adds to the top, Pop removes from the top, Peek looks without taking. Queues speak Enqueue/Dequeue instead.
Empty stack, wrong TIME to pop - InvalidOperationException (4.7's 'right arguments, wrong state'). TryPop returns false instead.

explanation: LIFO reverses for free - last pushed, first popped. 5.6 uses exactly this to fix binary digits coming out backwards.

stem: Why is a STACK the right tool for checking balanced brackets?
options: The most recent unclosed opener must close FIRST - exactly LIFO
explanation: Push openers; each closer must match the POP. Wrong kind or empty stack = unbalanced. This is how compilers check your braces.

stem: Which task naturally wants a QUEUE?
options: A print spooler - first submitted, first printed
explanation: First-come-first-served = FIFO. Undo, back-buttons and call frames are LIFO; spoolers, buffers and BFS are queues.

options: "chest pain" - LOWEST priority number comes out first
explanation: PriorityQueue serves smallest-priority first. Dijkstra (5.8) is built on exactly this collection.

stem: Using list.RemoveAt(0) as 'dequeue' is bad because:
options: Every removal shuffles the whole list left - O(n) each time; Queue<T> is O(1)
explanation: The array underneath must close the gap. Queue<T> uses a circular buffer (built from scratch in 5.6) and never shuffles.

stem: Why does chain[2] not exist on a LinkedList<int>?
options: No index arithmetic exists - nodes are scattered, reachable only by walking pointers
explanation: Linked lists trade O(1) indexing for O(1) inserts at known nodes. And honestly: List<T> usually beats it anyway - you study it because trees are built from the same idea.

explanation: Back = most recent first (Stack); typed keys processed in order (Queue); uniqueness with fast membership (HashSet).
